opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing to recognize is that "open source" in AI today mostly means open weights. You get the final artifact, but you don't get the training data, the data pipelines, or really the full recipe. That's useful, but it's not open source the way we understand it in software, where anyone can inspect, reproduce, and improve the whole thing.

As open models get closer to the frontier, that gap matters more. If these models end up mediating how people get information, make decisions, and manage their money, we need to be able to verify what went into them and how they behave. So I think the next phase has to be about openness across the whole stack: data provenance, training code, evaluation, and the ability to audit all of it.

The second piece is incentives. Right now open models are mostly released by large companies or well-funded labs, and they can decide tomorrow to stop. That isn't a sustainable foundation. We need ways for the people contributing to these models, whether that's data, compute, or research, to actually be rewarded and to have ownership. That's where I think crypto and decentralized coordination can play a real role: funding training runs collectively, tracking contributions, and letting the community govern the model instead of one company.

And third, privacy and user ownership. If AI is going to act on your behalf, it has to work for you, not for whoever is serving it. That means things like confidential compute, so you can run inference on sensitive data without the provider seeing it, and models and agents that are actually owned by the user.

So to me it's moving from "here are some weights you can download" to genuinely user-owned AI, which is open, verifiable, privately runnable, and collectively built.

r001.rationale: It calls for rewarding contributors and giving them ownership, but does not identify a monetization gap for developers who openly release models.

r002.rationale: It says AI “open source” mostly means open weights, while training data, data pipelines, and the full recipe are withheld.

r003.rationale: It does not say that undisclosed development processes waste resources by making others repeat experiments.

r004.rationale: It proposes openness across the whole stack, including training code, as an advance beyond releasing weights alone.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the interesting thing is that "open source" in AI has mostly meant open weights, right? Somebody trains a model, they put the weights on Hugging Face, and we call it open. And that's great, I'm glad it exists, but it's not really open source in the way we understood it with Linux or Kubernetes. You can't look at the data, you usually can't reproduce the training run, and most importantly you can't really participate in making the next version. You're a consumer of whatever the lab decides to release, and the lab can stop releasing whenever its business model changes.

So as open models get close to the frontier, I actually think the question shifts. It's less "can we match the quality" and more "who owns this and who decides what it does." Because once the capability gap closes, the thing that matters is the governance. If the best open model is still produced by one company in one jurisdiction, with one set of incentives, then we've just moved the single point of control, we haven't removed it.

What I'd like to see change is a few things. One, we need to open up the whole pipeline, not just the artifact. Data provenance, training code, evals, the recipe. Two, we need a way for people to actually contribute compute, data, and work, and get credit for it, so that the model is built by many parties instead of released by one. That's a coordination problem, and honestly it's a problem of incentives and attribution more than a technical one, which is why I spend so much time on the crypto side of this. Three, I think we have to take seriously that these models become infrastructure. People build businesses on them, governments will run on them. Infrastructure that one party can switch off or quietly change is a fragile thing to build on. So "user owned" AI, where the people who depend on the model also have a say in it and a right to keep running it, is where I think this needs to go.

And the last piece, which people underrate, is that open models catching up removes the argument that you need to be closed for safety. If the capability is going to be out there anyway, the safer world is the one where you can actually inspect it, run it locally, verify what it does with your data. So I'd flip the framing. Open source doesn't need to change in order to catch up. It needs to change so that, once it has caught up, we end up with something that's genuinely owned by the community rather than just free to download for now.

r001.rationale: The response discusses incentives, attribution, and business models, but does not identify a monetization gap for developers who openly release models.

r002.rationale: It says AI openness has mostly meant publishing weights while the data and training code remain unavailable.

r003.rationale: It says training runs are hard to reproduce, but does not explain that this wastes resources by forcing others to repeat experiments.

r004.rationale: It proposes opening the whole pipeline, including training code, evaluations, and the training recipe, rather than releasing only the model artifact.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to move from open models to an open process for building AI. Publishing weights is valuable, but there’s a lot around those weights: how you collect data, how you evaluate the model, how you improve it, and how people can contribute.

As open models catch up, the question becomes: can a community iterate faster than a single company? For that, you need ways for people to contribute different pieces—data, compute, evaluations, expertise—and have those contributions fit together. Someone who understands a particular language or domain should be able to improve the system without having to train an entire model themselves.

And there’s an economic question, too. How do you sustain that work? How do contributors share in the value they create? If we can make collaboration both practical and sustainable, then open source becomes much more than a way to distribute models. It becomes a way to build them together.

r001.rationale: The response raises sustainability and sharing value with contributors, but does not identify a monetization gap for developers who openly release AI models.

r002.rationale: It says publishing weights is valuable and mentions the work around them, but does not say that releases increasingly withhold the source used to develop the models.

r003.rationale: The response does not explain that closed development processes force others to repeat experiments or waste resources.

r004.rationale: It explicitly advocates moving from open models to an open process for building AI, beyond merely publishing weights.

sol-6.1.text:
I think open source needs to become more than releasing the weights. That’s an important step, but if people can’t understand how a model was built, evaluate it, or meaningfully contribute to improving it, you still have a fairly closed development process around an open artifact.

As open models catch up, the question becomes: how do we organize the work? Training requires compute, but it also requires data, experimentation, evaluation, and feedback from people using these systems. We need ways for more people to contribute across that whole process, and incentives that make those contributions sustainable.

And I think we should look beyond a single benchmark score. Can somebody adapt the model to their language? Can they run it at a reasonable cost? Can they inspect what happens to their data? Those are areas where an open ecosystem can deliver a lot of value.

So the opportunity is to move from a few organizations publishing models to a much broader community actually building them together. Releasing weights enables that, but it doesn’t automatically make it happen.

r001.rationale: The response calls for sustainable incentives but does not identify a monetization gap for developers who release models openly.

r002.rationale: It says weight releases alone can leave development closed, but does not observe that releases are increasingly exposing weights while withholding development source.

r003.rationale: It does not say that undisclosed development wastes resources by making others repeat experiments.

r004.rationale: It proposes going beyond releasing weights by making the development process open to understanding and contribution across the whole process.
